paragraphs: Large neural networks can represent complicated functions, but evaluating every part of a dense network can make inference expensive. Sparsely activated networks address this by routing each input through only part of the model. This paper develops a formal description of that arrangement, capturing important features of architectures in which the input determines which subnetwork is used.

The main theoretical result is a construction of sparse networks that match dense networks in approximation power and total size for Lipschitz functions, whose outputs change at a bounded rate as inputs change. These sparse constructions require substantially fewer operations during inference. The central technique uses locality sensitive hashing to organize inputs, followed by interpolation within different parts of the input space.

This distinguishes the total capacity a network stores from the amount of computation it uses for one prediction. The result supplies a theoretical explanation for how sparse activation can preserve approximation quality while reducing active computation. Experiments support this account by showing a favorable balance between the number of active units and approximation quality.
neurips-2022-a-theoretical-view-on-spars.tldr: The paper constructs sparse networks that match dense-network approximation power for Lipschitz functions while using fewer inference operations.

paragraphs: A classifier deployed over time may encounter changing proportions of classes without receiving new labels. This paper studies that situation under a specific assumption: class frequencies may change, but the distribution of inputs within each class stays fixed. A model is initially trained on labeled offline data and must then adapt using an unlabeled stream.

The authors construct an unbiased estimator of prediction risk from the unlabeled observations. This provides a way to assess decisions despite the absence of direct supervision, although the resulting estimation problem can be nonconvex. They then build online ensemble algorithms that use this foundation to respond to changes in the environment.

The theoretical guarantee concerns dynamic regret, which compares accumulated performance with an ideal decision-maker that knows the environments afterward and selects the best decision at each round. The authors obtain an optimal bound that depends on both the intensity and pattern of the label shifts. This captures adaptation to changing conditions within the stated label-shift setting. Experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the approach's effectiveness.
neurips-2022-adapting-to-online-label-sh.tldr: Online ensemble algorithms adapt to changing class frequencies using unlabeled data, with optimal dynamic-regret guarantees under label-shift assumptions.

paragraphs: Data poisoning is usually discussed as a way to damage a model's accuracy or induce particular wrong predictions. This paper investigates a different consequence: making it easier to determine whether legitimate examples were part of the training data. The attacks target membership exposure for a chosen class, linking manipulation of training data to privacy risks for otherwise benign samples.

The authors introduce two forms of poisoning. One is a generic dirty-label attack for supervised classification, involving incorrectly labeled poison examples. The other is an optimization-based clean-label attack in a transfer-learning setting. In the latter, the injected examples retain correct labels and appear natural, with the aim of avoiding detection through human moderation.

Evaluations on computer vision benchmarks show substantial increases in membership-inference precision with minimal degradation of overall test performance. This means a model can continue to appear effective on its main prediction task while becoming more revealing about its training data. The paper also investigates feasible countermeasures, treating privacy exposure as a poisoning outcome that merits attention alongside predictive accuracy.
neurips-2022-amplifying-membership-expos.tldr: Data poisoning can substantially increase training-data membership exposure while causing little overall loss of prediction performance.

paragraphs: With a fixed training-compute budget, language-model developers must balance model size against the amount of text used for training. This paper investigates that balance through more than 400 models, ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters and trained on 5 to 500 billion tokens. The authors find that the large models they discuss are substantially undertrained.

Their empirical analysis indicates that compute-optimal scaling should increase model size and training tokens together: doubling the parameter count should also double the token count. They test this prediction with Chinchilla, a 70-billion-parameter model trained using the same compute budget as Gopher but four times as much data. Gopher has 280 billion parameters.

Chinchilla significantly outperforms Gopher and the other named large models across a broad range of downstream evaluations. It reaches 67.5% average accuracy on MMLU, reported as a 7% improvement over Gopher. Its smaller size also reduces fine-tuning and inference compute. The findings make data allocation a central part of efficient model scaling, with benefits extending beyond the initial training run.
neurips-2022-an-empirical-analysis-of-co.tldr: An empirical scaling study finds that increasing training data alongside model size yields better use of compute, as demonstrated by Chinchilla.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to functions that are expensive to evaluate. Traditional approaches choose queries sequentially, using a probabilistic model of the function and an acquisition function that scores possible evaluations. BORE reformulates this scoring process through density-ratio estimation, allowing a probabilistic binary classifier to play the acquisition role without an explicit prior over functions.

This paper develops the theoretical foundations of that reformulation by analyzing BORE's regret, a measure of the shortfall associated with its optimization decisions. It also proposes an extension with improved uncertainty estimates. That uncertainty component matters because choosing where to evaluate requires more than a prediction of which inputs currently appear promising.

The authors further extend BORE to selecting batches of query points by expressing the task as approximate Bayesian inference. This connects the classifier-based formulation to a setting where multiple evaluations can be chosen together. The resulting algorithms have theoretical performance guarantees and are evaluated against batch and sequential Bayesian-optimization methods. The contribution combines analysis, uncertainty estimation, and batch selection within the same overall approach.
neurips-2022-batch-bayesian-optimisation.tldr: The paper gives BORE theoretical guarantees, improves its uncertainty estimates, and extends its classifier-based optimization approach to batch selection.

paragraphs: An associative memory retrieves a stored observation from an incomplete or corrupted version of it. The paper argues that recent machine-learning work has emphasized retrieval more than the process of adding new memories. BayesPCN addresses the writing side by introducing a hierarchical memory that can continually store observations after seeing them once, without relying on meta-learning.

The model also supports gradual forgetting of previous observations to free memory. Writing, recall, and forgetting therefore appear as complementary capabilities of the same system. This matters for continual memory use: the model is designed to incorporate incoming observations over time, while also providing a mechanism for releasing capacity occupied by older ones.

Experiments examine recall of corrupted, high-dimensional observations drawn independently from the same distribution. BayesPCN retrieves data encountered hundreds to a thousand time steps earlier without a large decline in recall relative to leading parametric memories trained offline. The stated finding is that continual one-shot writing can coexist with strong delayed recall in this experimental setting, bringing attention to how memories are learned as well as read.
neurips-2022-bayespcn-a-continually-lear.tldr: BayesPCN combines continual one-shot memory writing, gradual forgetting, and strong recall of corrupted observations from hundreds of time steps earlier.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples created against one neural network may fail against another because they exploit details specific to the first model. This paper studies how to improve that transfer, which matters when the eventual target's architecture or parameters are unknown. Its proposed method, reverse adversarial perturbation, aims to reduce overfitting to the surrogate network used to generate the examples.

Instead of optimizing only the attack loss at a single point, RAP seeks a surrounding region with consistently low loss. Each optimization step introduces a worst-case reverse perturbation, producing a two-level min-max problem. The intended result is an adversarial example whose effectiveness is less sensitive to changes in the model's decision boundary.

Experiments show significant improvements in transferability, and RAP can be incorporated into several existing black-box attack techniques for further gains. On the Google Cloud Vision image-recognition system, the authors report a 22% improvement in targeted-attack performance over the compared method. These findings support the idea that stability around an adversarial example can improve its ability to affect a different model.
neurips-2022-boosting-the-transferabilit.tldr: Reverse adversarial perturbation improves attack transfer by seeking adversarial examples that remain effective throughout a surrounding region.

paragraphs: CAGroup3D detects three-dimensional objects in point clouds using a two-stage framework built from sparse convolutions. Its first stage forms candidate objects by grouping surface voxels that share semantic predictions. This grouping accounts for both agreement about object class and varied local spatial structure, addressing aspects the authors identify as neglected by earlier bottom-up methods.

The second stage addresses information lost when individual voxels receive incorrect semantic labels. A sparse region-of-interest pooling module gathers detailed spatial features directly from the backbone network to refine each proposal. This lets refinement use geometric evidence that the initial grouping may have missed, rather than depending entirely on the correctness of the first-stage segmentation.

The authors describe the approach as efficient in both memory and computation, with improved encoding of each proposal's geometry. They report state-of-the-art detection results, including gains of +3.6% on ScanNet V2 and +2.6% on SUN RGB-D in mAP@0.25. The overall design pairs semantically informed proposal generation with a refinement stage specifically intended to recover spatial information excluded earlier.
neurips-2022-cagroup3d-class-aware-group.tldr: CAGroup3D improves point-cloud object detection through class-aware grouping followed by sparse refinement that recovers missed spatial features.

paragraphs: A training example can be difficult because its label is wrong, because it belongs to a rare group, or because its underlying pattern is complex. Common measures of learning and forgetting do not reliably separate these explanations. This paper introduces second-split forgetting time, which examines what happens to previously learned examples when training moves to another portion of the data.

The method first learns from one split, then fine-tunes on a randomly held-out partition. It records the epoch, if any, after which an original training example is forgotten. Across several datasets and data types, mislabeled examples are forgotten quickly, while examples that appear rare are forgotten more slowly. Measures restricted to the initial learning phase struggle to make this distinction.

At large learning rates, the measure tends to remain robust across architectures, optimizers, and random seeds. The authors show that it can help identify mislabeled examples whose removal improves generalization, and can illuminate model failure modes. A theoretical analysis of overparameterized linear models offers an explanation for how the observed differences in forgetting may arise.
neurips-2022-characterizing-datapoints-v.tldr: Tracking forgetting after a switch to held-out training data helps distinguish mislabeled examples from seemingly rare ones.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis identifies a direction capturing prominent variation in data. This paper studies estimating the principal component from independent, identically distributed samples while satisfying differential privacy. The motivation is a gap between private and nonprivate estimation: the authors describe existing private algorithms as needing substantially more samples to obtain useful results, even for Gaussian data.

In the comparison presented, earlier private methods require sample counts scaling at least as d to the three-halves power, where d is the data dimension, while nonprivate PCA needs only order d samples. Existing techniques also incur large errors even when individual data points have small variance. DP-PCA addresses these issues with a single-pass procedure resembling minibatch gradient descent.

For sub-Gaussian data, the authors establish nearly optimal statistical error rates with sample counts on the order of d log d. This brings the stated sample requirement much closer to the linear dependence available without privacy. The result shows that strong statistical performance and differential privacy can be combined more efficiently for this estimation problem under the specified data assumptions.
neurips-2022-dp-pca-statistically-optima.tldr: DP-PCA achieves nearly optimal private principal-component estimation for sub-Gaussian data using a single pass and roughly d log d samples.

paragraphs: Generating an image in a single direction can limit how much each decision reflects the image's overall context. This paper proposes a generation framework that first creates a draft and then revises it. The aim is to make global image information available during generation, while retaining control over both visual quality and the variety of produced images.

An RQ-VAE represents a high-resolution image as a sequence of discrete code stacks. During training, some stacks are randomly hidden, and a Contextual RQ-Transformer learns to fill them in using the visible portions of the image. This makes contextual completion the model's central learning task and provides the basis for its two-phase decoding procedure.

The draft phase emphasizes diverse outputs even when their initial quality is low. The revision phase repeatedly improves quality while preserving the generated image's global context. Experiments report state-of-the-art conditional image-generation results and show that the decoding procedure can achieve strong performance by managing the quality-diversity trade-off. The contribution links contextual training with a generation process that can revisit and improve an initial image.
neurips-2022-draft-and-revise-effective-.tldr: A Contextual RQ-Transformer generates diverse image drafts and iteratively revises them using global context to improve quality.

paragraphs: Data can occupy a structured, lower-dimensional shape within the space used to represent it. This paper asks how that geometry affects a neural network at random initialization. It studies networks with piecewise linear activations, which divide their inputs into regions where the network acts as a linear function, and examines those regions along the data manifold.

The authors derive bounds on the density of region boundaries and on distances to those boundaries when measured on the manifold. These quantities describe how the network's linear behavior changes across the space where data actually lie. The analysis therefore connects expressivity at initialization to data geometry, including settings where that geometry is non-Euclidean.

Experiments on a toy supervised-learning problem support the theoretical results: the number of linear regions varies across manifolds, with the findings persisting across changes in network architecture. An additional study using MetFaces shows that region complexity on the image manifold differs from complexity in the surrounding Euclidean space. Together, these results make the structure of the data part of the account of early network expressivity.
neurips-2022-effects-of-data-geometry-in.tldr: The geometry of the data manifold affects how randomly initialized piecewise linear networks divide data into linear regions.

paragraphs: Optimization methods may receive exact information about an objective or noisy information from a stochastic source. Extra-Newton is designed to adapt between these situations when minimizing convex functions with second-order smoothness. As a second-order method, it uses information about curvature, and its central contribution is a convergence guarantee that changes with the feedback without requiring its nature in advance.

For stochastic oracle feedback with variance denoted by sigma in the abstract, the algorithm achieves a rate of O(sigma / sqrt(T)). With a deterministic oracle, it achieves the faster rate O(1 / T^3). Here T represents the number of optimization steps. The same method interpolates between these guarantees rather than requiring the user to select a separate algorithm for each setting.

The enabling mechanism is a parameter-free step size that does not require the smoothness modulus, variance bounds, or diameter of the constrained set. This removes several pieces of advance information from algorithm tuning. Within second-order convex optimization, the authors identify the combination of these global guarantees and automatic adaptation as the first such result to their knowledge.
neurips-2022-extra-newton-a-first-approa.tldr: Extra-Newton automatically adapts its convergence rate to stochastic or deterministic feedback without prior knowledge of key optimization parameters.

paragraphs: Broad capabilities in foundation models do not necessarily translate into understanding specialized technical material. This paper introduces FETA to evaluate such understanding through matching illustrations with language descriptions. Its motivation is that expert content may be absent or sparsely represented in pretraining data, leaving tasks such as retrieving technical illustrations poorly served by standard evaluations.

FETA focuses on text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval using public car manuals and sales catalogue brochures. It includes a fully automatic procedure for extracting annotations, making extension to other document types and application domains easier. The resulting automated performance metric is shown to be consistent with metrics based on human-curated annotations.

The authors provide multiple baselines and analyze popular foundation models on the benchmark. The contribution is an evaluation setting centered on technical documentation, together with a scalable way to construct its annotations. This makes specialized matching tasks available for explicit evaluation and fine-tuning, broadening attention beyond the common objects emphasized by standard benchmarks and toward the visual-language relationships encountered in expert documents.
neurips-2022-feta-towards-specializing-f.tldr: FETA benchmarks foundation models on matching technical illustrations and text, using automatically extracted annotations from automotive documents.

paragraphs: Federated clients may belong to distinct groups whose data follow different predictive relationships. This paper studies that structure through mixed regression: each client's local data come from one of k unknown regression models. The challenge includes severe imbalance in local sample counts, with some clients potentially holding only a constant number of observations.

The algorithm begins by applying moment descent to a small set of anchor clients, each with roughly k samples up to logarithmic factors, to obtain coarse model estimates. It then alternates between estimating clients' cluster assignments and refining the regression models using FedAvg or FedProx. This combines a structured initialization procedure with repeated assignment and model updates.

The authors prove global convergence from any initialization in the studied setting, including the stated local-data imbalance. The anchor clients supply an explicit source of information even when many other clients have very little data. A central analytical contribution is a uniform bound on clustering errors, obtained using VC-dimension bounds for polynomial concept classes and tools from algebraic geometry.
neurips-2022-global-convergence-of-feder.tldr: A federated mixed-regression algorithm achieves global convergence using anchor clients and alternating clustering and model refinement, despite highly uneven local data.

paragraphs: A model can learn accidental associations that work in its training environment but fail elsewhere. Invariance learning aims to find predictors that remain useful across environments, usually by requiring training data from several domains. This paper reduces the demand for expensive target-task annotations by making use of a hierarchy of classification labels.

The framework assumes that data from multiple domains are available for a higher-level classification task whose labels cost less to obtain. For the target task, training examples need come from only one domain. The method uses the broader task's cross-domain information to estimate an invariant predictor for the more specific task, connecting annotation availability across levels of the hierarchy.

The authors also propose two cross-validation procedures for choosing the strength of invariance regularization. Experiments demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, including this model-selection component. The theory shows that the desired invariant predictor can be estimated when the hyperparameter is correctly fixed, and that the proposed cross-validation methods select a suitable value under stated conditions. Thus both the learning result and parameter-selection result retain explicit qualifications.
neurips-2022-invariance-learning-based-o.tldr: Label hierarchies enable invariant learning with target-task data from one domain, provided higher-level labeled data span multiple domains.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural models can benefit from encoding the structure of mechanical laws, but earlier Lagrangian and Hamiltonian networks largely addressed simple systems or individual rigid bodies. This paper introduces a Lagrangian graph neural network for articulated systems made from connected rigid components. It uses the system's connection topology as part of learning how that system moves.

The authors demonstrate the approach on ropes, chains, and trusses, modeling bars as rigid bodies. A central result concerns generalization across structure: a model trained on chains with few segments can simulate chains with many links and arbitrary link lengths. They also demonstrate simulation of previously unseen hybrid systems that combine bars and chains.

These results show how physical structure and graph connectivity can support reuse of learned dynamics beyond the particular assemblies seen in training. The paper also applies the model to complex structures, including tensegrity stability. Finally, it discusses the mass matrix's non-diagonal structure and its relationship to generalization in complex systems, connecting the model's physical representation with its ability to handle interacting components.
neurips-2022-learning-articulated-rigid-.tldr: A Lagrangian graph neural network learns connected rigid-body dynamics and demonstrates generalization to larger chains and unseen combinations of components.

paragraphs: Planning a robot's motion around moving obstacles requires reasoning about both location and timing. A route that is clear at one moment may be blocked at another, making the search space much larger than in a static environment. This paper develops a learned approach to accelerate planning in dynamic settings such as multi-arm assembly and human-robot interaction.

The method combines a graph neural network with temporal encoding. It uses imitation learning with data aggregation to learn both representations and policies for prioritizing graph edges. Edge prioritization directs the planner's search effort, while temporal encoding incorporates the time-dependent information needed to reason about interactions with moving obstacles.

Experiments show significant online-planning acceleration relative to leading complete dynamic-planning algorithms. The learned models often reduce expensive collision checks by more than a factor of 1,000 and achieve planning acceleration of up to 95%, while retaining high success rates on difficult instances. These are reported experimental outcomes, highlighting how learned search priorities can reduce the costly geometric checking involved in dynamic motion planning.
neurips-2022-learning-based-motion-plann.tldr: A graph neural network with temporal encoding learns search priorities that substantially accelerate motion planning around moving obstacles in experiments.

paragraphs: Myriad is a JAX testbed for comparing learning-based control with trajectory optimization. It contains 17 continuous-time optimal-control problems spanning medicine, ecology, epidemiology, and engineering. By putting these problems and methods into a shared software setting, the authors aim to make it easier to evaluate imitation learning and reinforcement learning on tasks motivated by practical applications.

The package also exposes trajectory-optimization tools for independent use or integration into automatic-differentiation workflows. Its GPU-compatible design connects classical control techniques with deep-learning machinery. This matters because optimization can become a component within a trainable system, alongside its role as a method against which learned controllers are benchmarked.

The paper demonstrates that integration through an end-to-end model for dynamics learning and control. An implicit planning module operates over neural ordinary differential equations, allowing the model to learn unknown environment dynamics and plan simultaneously. Myriad's contribution therefore includes both a collection of control problems and a concrete example of combining learning with planning. The software provides the environments, optimizers, and associated tools.
neurips-2022-myriad-a-real-world-testbed.tldr: Myriad provides 17 continuous-time control benchmarks and differentiable optimization tools, including an end-to-end approach to learning dynamics while planning.

paragraphs: Collecting too much training data wastes resources, while collecting too little can delay a project and create additional costs later. This paper treats data collection as an optimization problem with explicit performance targets, collection costs, a planning horizon, and penalties for missing the targets. The formulation makes the consequences of collection decisions part of the learning workflow.

It also accommodates tasks that draw on several data sources, including the combination of labeled and unlabeled examples in semi-supervised learning. The proposed Learn-Optimize-Collect method minimizes expected future collection costs. This shifts the decision from simply estimating a final dataset size to optimizing collection under the specified costs and performance requirements.

The authors compare their framework numerically with the conventional approach of extrapolating data needs from neural scaling laws. Across several classification, segmentation, and detection tasks, it substantially reduces the risk of missing desired performance targets while maintaining low total collection costs. The findings support planning data acquisition around both achievement risk and expenditure, making explicit the trade-off between collecting now and potentially paying more later.
neurips-2022-optimizing-data-collection-.tldr: Learn-Optimize-Collect plans data acquisition around costs and performance targets, reducing target-miss risk while keeping collection costs low in experiments.

paragraphs: Injective attacks manipulate recommender systems by adding fake users with designed behavior, aiming to promote a target item to real users. This paper revisits how such attacks allocate a limited fake-user budget. It identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches: excessive effort directed at users unlikely to favor the target, and insufficient diversity in the communities reached.

The proposed attacker, DADA, introduces objectives that account for both difficulty and diversity. It gives greater weight to easier users across different communities during optimization. The purpose is to focus on users more receptive to the target item while avoiding fake behavior patterns dominated by large communities, which can narrow an attack's reach.

Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed attacker's effectiveness. The underlying finding is that susceptibility and community coverage need to be considered together when assessing how fake-user behavior influences recommendations. Concentrating on easier users can improve the use of a limited attack budget, while the diversity objective helps the attack affect a broader range of real users.
neurips-2022-revisiting-injective-attack.tldr: DADA improves fake-user recommendation attacks by emphasizing receptive users across diverse communities.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to recover reward signals that explain demonstrated behavior. Adversarial imitation methods provide a scalable approach, but the paper argues that directly tackling difficult optimization problems can produce uncertain rewards and unreliable learning. Its proposed remedy is to learn a sequence of reward functions through updates inspired by mirror descent.

Each reward update is an iterative solution to a constrained convex problem. Local geometric constraints regulate how much reward learning occurs, making the resulting inverse-reinforcement-learning solutions tolerant of uncertainty in target-density estimation. The method therefore ties robustness to the way updates are controlled, rather than treating reward estimation as a single direct optimization task.

The authors prove that their mirror-descent update robustly minimizes a Bregman divergence, a measure of discrepancy used in the analysis, with an O(1/T) regret bound for the considered step-size sequence. They then place the method within an adversarial learning framework and report improvements over existing adversarial methods across an extensive benchmark suite. The contribution connects a controlled reward-learning procedure with both a formal robustness result and empirical imitation performance.
neurips-2022-robust-imitation-via-mirror.tldr: Mirror-descent reward updates improve robustness to estimation uncertainty in inverse reinforcement learning, with a regret guarantee and stronger benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with interacting parts, and some combinations may violate known rules. This paper introduces a Semantic Probabilistic Layer that can be attached to a neural network to guarantee consistency with predefined symbolic constraints. The layer is designed to represent both complex dependencies among outputs and rules that must always be satisfied.

Its mechanism combines exact probabilistic inference with logical reasoning. The learned distribution assigns support only to outputs that satisfy the constraints, while allowing the full network to be trained end to end through maximum likelihood. This places validity inside the predictive model itself and gives the model room to learn correlations among the remaining permissible outputs.

Experiments cover hierarchical multi-label classification, pathfinding, and preference learning. The authors report higher accuracy than competing neuro-symbolic approaches while maintaining perfect constraint satisfaction. These results distinguish two aspects of success: obeying the specified rules and choosing accurate outputs among those rules' valid solutions. The paper's contribution is a modular layer that addresses both aspects within a probabilistic learning framework.
neurips-2022-semantic-probabilistic-laye.tldr: Semantic Probabilistic Layers learn structured predictions while guaranteeing compliance with predefined symbolic constraints.

paragraphs: Speaker-recognition systems can identify people from audio, motivating methods that alter speech to reduce identity exposure. Adversarial audio often requires slow offline optimization, making it awkward for live streams. VoiceBlock instead trains an audio-to-audio neural network to modify outgoing speech in real time, drawing inspiration from speech enhancement and denoising architectures.

The model learns a time-varying finite impulse response filter that applies perturbations with a small, fixed delay. This design makes streaming operation part of the method itself. The authors demonstrate effective de-identification against speaker recognition and show that the modifications can transfer to an unseen recognition system.

A perceptual study compares the method with baseline anonymization approaches while controlling for effectiveness. Under that comparison, VoiceBlock's perturbations are significantly less perceptible. The authors also provide an implementation that runs in real time on a single CPU thread. Together, the findings address both identity disruption and practical listening and deployment requirements, showing that a learned audio transformation can combine low delay with relatively inconspicuous modifications.
neurips-2022-voiceblock-privacy-through-.tldr: VoiceBlock modifies streaming speech in real time to disrupt speaker recognition with comparatively inconspicuous audio changes.

paragraphs: Predicting a critical event does not by itself determine when an intervention should occur. This paper formulates timing directly: minimize the expected time remaining until the event when intervention happens, subject to a bound on the probability of missing it. That objective captures a preference for intervening close to the event while controlling the risk of waiting too long.

The authors introduce a hazard rate process to describe how event risk evolves with observations of system behavior. They show that the intervention problem is equivalent to an optimal stopping problem on this process. Under Markovian assumptions, the optimal policy at a given time can be determined analytically from the conditional hazard rate function.

The theory also covers a class of neural hazard processes generated by recurrent networks. To model these, the authors introduce dynamic deep recurrent survival analysis, adding a recurrent encoder to the static DRSA setting. Experiments show that the resulting recurrent-network intervention policies outperform popular intervention methods. The contribution connects risk modeling to an explicit timing objective and derives the decision rule under the stated assumptions.
neurips-2022-when-to-intervene-learning-.tldr: The paper derives intervention timing as an optimal stopping problem and learns recurrent risk models to support the resulting policies.
